name: Beaker
description: A general-purpose laboratory container used for holding, mixing, heating and transferring liquids.
info: A beaker is a common laboratory glass container. Its graduations are approximate, so it is not intended for high-precision volume measurement.

name: Test Tube
description: A small glass tube used for reactions, heating and observing small samples.
info: Test tubes are useful for small-scale reactions and for observing colour changes, precipitates and gas formation.

name: Conical Flask
description: A narrow-neck flask that makes swirling and mixing liquids easier.
info: A conical flask, or Erlenmeyer flask, is commonly used for mixing, solution preparation and titration.

name: Boiling Flask
description: A round-bottom flask designed for heating and boiling liquids.
info: A boiling flask is designed for heating liquids relatively evenly and is normally supported in a suitable heating setup.

name: Watch Glass
description: A shallow curved glass dish used for evaporation, covering and holding small samples.
info: A watch glass can hold small samples, cover a beaker and evaporate small quantities of liquid.

name: Crucible
description: A heat-resistant container used for strongly heating small quantities of solids.
info: A crucible is designed for high-temperature heating of substances and is commonly handled with suitable crucible tongs.

name: Funnel
description: Used to guide liquids into narrow containers and to support filter paper.
info: A laboratory funnel helps transfer liquids or fine solids into containers with small openings and can support filter paper during gravity filtration.

name: Measuring Cylinder
description: A graduated container used to measure liquid volume more accurately than a beaker.
info: A measuring cylinder is used to measure liquid volumes. Read the meniscus at eye level for the best classroom accuracy.

name: Volumetric Flask
description: Designed to prepare solutions to one precise volume.
info: A volumetric flask has a calibrated mark and is used when preparing solutions of accurately known concentration.

name: Pipette
description: A precision device used to transfer measured volumes of liquid.
info: A pipette transfers a measured amount of liquid accurately. Volumetric pipettes deliver a fixed volume, while graduated pipettes provide a range.

name: Burette
description: A graduated tube with a stopcock used to deliver controlled liquid volumes.
info: A burette is commonly used in titration. Its stopcock allows liquid to be delivered gradually and its graduations show the delivered volume.

name: Dropping Pipette
description: A dropper used to transfer small amounts of liquid one drop at a time.
info: A dropping pipette is useful for adding small quantities of liquid drop by drop. It is not normally used for precise volume measurement.

name: Ring Stand & Clamps
description: A support system used to hold laboratory apparatus securely.
info: Ring stands and clamps support equipment such as burettes, flasks, funnels and other apparatus at suitable positions.

name: Tongs & Forceps
description: Tools used to safely hold, grip and handle laboratory objects.
info: Tongs can hold suitable hot apparatus such as crucibles, while forceps are useful for handling small objects or samples.

name: Spatula
description: Used to transfer small quantities of solid chemicals.
info: A laboratory spatula helps scoop and transfer small amounts of solid chemicals while reducing direct contact.

name: Thermometer
description: An instrument used to measure temperature during experiments.
info: A laboratory thermometer measures temperature. Liquid-in-glass and digital thermometers are common laboratory types.

name: Bunsen Burner
description: A laboratory burner used to provide a controlled flame for heating.
info: A Bunsen burner provides a controllable flame for laboratory heating and should be used according to laboratory safety instructions.

name: Safety Goggles
description: Protective eyewear designed to help protect the eyes from laboratory hazards.
info: Safety goggles provide a barrier around the eyes against suitable chemical splashes, particles and other laboratory hazards.

name: Lab Coat
description: Protective clothing that helps shield skin and everyday clothes from laboratory spills.
info: A laboratory coat provides an additional protective layer. It does not replace other required protective equipment.

name: Chemical-Resistant Gloves
description: Protective gloves selected to reduce skin contact with laboratory chemicals.
info: Chemical-resistant gloves help protect hands from hazardous substances. Glove material should be selected for the particular chemical.

name: Litmus / Filter Paper
description: Litmus paper tests acidity or basicity, while filter paper separates insoluble solids from liquids.
info: Litmus paper changes colour in acidic or basic conditions. Filter paper lets liquid pass while retaining suitable insoluble particles during filtration.

name: Glass Rod
description: A solid glass rod used for stirring and guiding liquids during transfer.
info: A glass rod is commonly used for stirring solutions and can help guide liquid along a surface during careful pouring.

name: Wash Bottle
description: A squeeze bottle used to dispense distilled or deionised water.
info: Wash bottles provide a controlled stream of water for rinsing glassware and washing residues from laboratory equipment.

name: Mortar & Pestle
description: Used to crush and grind solid substances into smaller particles or powder.
info: A mortar and pestle are used to grind suitable solid substances and improve contact between particles when appropriate.

name: Tripod Stand
description: A three-legged support used to hold apparatus above a heat source.
info: A tripod stand supports wire gauze, evaporating dishes or other suitable apparatus during laboratory heating.

name: Wire Gauze
description: A metal mesh support that helps distribute heat beneath glassware.
info: Wire gauze is placed on a suitable support to hold vessels above a burner and distribute heat more evenly.

name: Evaporating Dish
description: A heat-resistant dish used to evaporate solvent from a solution.
info: An evaporating dish is used for controlled evaporation of suitable solutions and for concentrating or recovering dissolved solids.

name: Balance
description: An instrument used to determine the mass of laboratory samples.
info: Laboratory balances measure mass. The balance type and its resolution determine how precisely a sample can be measured.

name: Separating Funnel
description: Used to separate immiscible liquid layers based on differences in density.
info: A separating funnel allows immiscible liquids to form layers and be separated through its stopcock.

name: Filter Flask
description: A thick-walled flask commonly used with vacuum filtration equipment.
info: A filter flask has a side arm for connection to suitable filtration equipment and is commonly used for vacuum-assisted filtration.

name: Gas Jar
description: A glass container used to collect, hold or demonstrate properties of gases.
info: Gas jars are used for collecting and demonstrating gases in school laboratory experiments.

name: Reagent Bottle
description: A labelled bottle designed for storing laboratory reagents.
info: Reagent bottles are used to store chemicals safely with suitable labels, closures and handling procedures.

name: Spatula Scoop
description: A small scoop-like tool used to transfer solid chemicals.
info: A spatula scoop is useful for taking small quantities of solid reagents from containers while reducing direct contact.

name: Watch Glass / Petri Dish
description: Shallow laboratory vessels used for holding, observing or covering small samples.
info: Watch glasses and Petri dishes are useful for holding small samples, observing materials and carrying out suitable small-scale activities.

name: Retort Stand
description: A vertical support stand used with clamps to hold laboratory apparatus.
info: A retort stand provides a stable vertical support for clamps and suitable laboratory equipment.

name: Dropper Bottle
description: A bottle fitted with a dropper for dispensing small quantities of liquid.
info: Dropper bottles are convenient for dispensing small amounts of suitable reagents or indicator solutions drop by drop.

name: Hydrochloric Acid
description: Strong mineral acid used in acid-base reactions, qualitative analysis and salt preparation.
info: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid in aqueous solution. It is commonly encountered in school acid-base and qualitative-analysis work.

name: Sulfuric Acid
description: A strong mineral acid used in selected laboratory reactions and preparation work.
info: Sulfuric acid is a strong acid and must be handled only under appropriate laboratory supervision and safety procedures.

name: Nitric Acid
description: A strong acid used in selected qualitative and inorganic chemistry tests.
info: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising acid and requires appropriate laboratory controls and protective equipment.

name: Acetic Acid
description: A weak organic acid commonly used in acid-base and organic chemistry studies.
info: Acetic acid is a weak acid. Dilute solutions are commonly encountered in educational chemistry.

name: Oxalic Acid
description: A laboratory acid used in standard solution preparation and titration studies.
info: Oxalic acid is commonly used as a primary-standard substance in school titration work where specified by the practical syllabus.

name: Benzoic Acid
description: An aromatic carboxylic acid used in organic chemistry and crystallisation studies.
info: Benzoic acid is a common solid organic acid and may be used in crystallisation experiments.

name: Dilute Hydrochloric Acid
description: Aqueous hydrochloric acid used in many school laboratory tests.
info: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used where an aqueous acidic medium is required in qualitative and reaction studies.

name: Dilute Sulfuric Acid
description: Aqueous sulfuric acid used in selected school laboratory reactions.
info: Dilute sulfuric acid provides an acidic medium for suitable classroom experiments.

name: Sodium Hydroxide
description: A strong base used in neutralisation, titration and qualitative analysis.
info: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base. It reacts with acids in neutralisation reactions and is used in several laboratory tests.

name: Ammonium Hydroxide
description: Aqueous ammonia solution used as a weak base and qualitative-analysis reagent.
info: Ammonium hydroxide is the traditional school-lab name for aqueous ammonia and is used to provide OH⁻ in qualitative tests.

name: Calcium Hydroxide
description: A sparingly soluble base used in selected chemistry demonstrations and tests.
info: Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble in water and is used in selected acid-base and qualitative chemistry contexts.

name: Sodium Carbonate
description: A basic salt used in standard solution preparation and acid titration.

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
description: A bicarbonate salt used in acid-carbonate reaction studies.
info: Sodium hydrogen carbonate reacts with acids to produce carbon dioxide, water and a salt.

name: Sodium Chloride
description: A common salt used in solution preparation and selected laboratory studies.
info: Sodium chloride is a common ionic compound and is useful for preparing simple salt solutions.

name: Copper(II) Sulfate
description: A blue copper salt used in crystallisation and other school laboratory studies.
info: Copper(II) sulfate is commonly encountered as blue crystals and is used in crystallisation and selected reactions.

name: Iron(II) Sulfate
description: An iron(II) salt used in selected inorganic and qualitative chemistry studies.
info: Iron(II) sulfate provides Fe²⁺ ions and is used in suitable laboratory tests and demonstrations.

name: Iron(III) Chloride
description: An iron(III) salt used in qualitative tests and equilibrium studies.
info: Iron(III) chloride provides Fe³⁺ ions and is used in selected qualitative-analysis and equilibrium experiments.

name: Barium Chloride
description: A soluble barium salt used for sulfate-ion testing.
info: Barium chloride can provide Ba²⁺ ions that form a characteristic insoluble sulfate precipitate in suitable tests.

name: Silver Nitrate
description: A silver salt used in selected halide and qualitative-analysis tests.
info: Silver nitrate provides Ag⁺ ions and is used for selected qualitative tests, including halide identification.

name: Lead Nitrate
description: A soluble lead salt used in selected qualitative-analysis demonstrations.
info: Lead nitrate provides Pb²⁺ ions. Lead compounds are hazardous and require appropriate supervised laboratory handling.

name: Potassium Chloride
description: A soluble potassium salt used in solution preparation and selected studies.
info: Potassium chloride is a common ionic salt used to provide K⁺ or Cl⁻ ions in suitable laboratory work.

name: Ammonium Chloride
description: An ammonium salt used in buffer-like mixtures and qualitative-analysis reagents.
info: Ammonium chloride is commonly used with ammonia solution in qualitative analysis to control the concentration of hydroxide ions.

name: Ammonium Sulfate
description: An ammonium salt used in selected inorganic and laboratory studies.
info: Ammonium sulfate is a soluble ionic salt containing ammonium and sulfate ions.

name: Mohr’s Salt
description: A stable iron(II) double salt used in redox titration studies.
info: Mohr's salt is a hydrated double salt of iron(II), ammonium and sulfate and is used in suitable redox practical work.

name: Aluminium Sulfate

name: Zinc Sulfate

name: Magnesium Sulfate

name: Calcium Chloride
description: A soluble calcium salt used in selected tests and solution preparation.
info: Calcium chloride is a common soluble salt and provides Ca²⁺ ions for suitable laboratory studies.

name: Potassium Sulfate
description: A soluble sulfate salt used in selected ionic and solution studies.

name: Silver Nitrate (Qualitative Reagent)

name: Glacial Acetic Acid

name: Acid–Base Neutralisation
description: Use an indicator to find the exact point where an acid cancels out an alkali.
info: Use an indicator to find the exact point where an acid cancels out an alkali. Equipment: Conical flask, Burette, Pipette, White tile, Funnel. Chemicals: Hydrochloric acid, Sodium hydroxide, Phenolphthalein. Procedure: Pipette 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask. Add 3 drops of phenolphthalein — the solution turns pink. Fill the burette with hydrochloric acid and note the starting volume. Add acid slowly, swirling, until the pink colour just disappears. Record the final burette reading and calculate the volume used. Observations: Solution starts pink; Colour fades near the end-point; Becomes colourless at neutralisation; Flask feels slightly warm Explanation: Hydrogen ions from the acid combine with hydroxide ions from the alkali to form water. Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in neutral/acid solution, so it signals when all the OH⁻ has been used up. Equation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O Conclusion: Neutralisation is exothermic and produces a salt and water. The volume of acid needed tells us the concentration of the alkali. Safety: Both reagents are corrosive — wear goggles throughout.

name: Metal Displacement
description: Drop zinc into blue copper sulfate and watch copper metal appear.
info: Drop zinc into blue copper sulfate and watch copper metal appear. Equipment: Test tubes, Test tube rack, Spatula, Thermometer. Chemicals: Copper(II) sulfate, Zinc, Iron, Magnesium. Procedure: Pour 5 cm³ of copper sulfate solution into three test tubes. Record the starting temperature. Add a spatula of zinc to the first, iron to the second, magnesium to the third. Observe for five minutes and record the highest temperature reached. Observations: Blue colour fades; Brown/pink copper coats the metal; Temperature rises — most with magnesium; Iron solution turns pale green Explanation: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Zinc, iron and magnesium are all above copper in the reactivity series, so they take the sulfate and release copper atoms. Equation: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu Conclusion: The larger the gap in reactivity, the more vigorous and more exothermic the displacement reaction. Safety: Copper sulfate is harmful — wash hands after the experiment.

name: Making & Testing Carbon Dioxide
description: React a carbonate with acid and prove the gas is CO₂ with limewater.
info: React a carbonate with acid and prove the gas is CO₂ with limewater. Equipment: Boiling tube, Delivery tube with bung, Test tube, Measuring cylinder. Chemicals: Sodium bicarbonate, Hydrochloric acid, Limewater. Procedure: Place a spatula of sodium bicarbonate in a boiling tube. Add 10 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid and quickly fit the delivery tube. Bubble the gas through a test tube of limewater. Observe the limewater. Observations: Vigorous fizzing; Limewater turns milky/cloudy; Boiling tube feels cool Explanation: Acids react with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to release carbon dioxide. CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide in limewater to form a fine white precipitate of calcium carbonate. Equation: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ ; CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O Conclusion: Limewater turning milky is the standard positive test for carbon dioxide. Safety: Keep the delivery tube out of the limewater before removing heat/pressure to avoid suck-back.

name: Elephant Toothpaste
description: A catalyst makes hydrogen peroxide erupt into a tower of warm foam.
info: A catalyst makes hydrogen peroxide erupt into a tower of warm foam. Equipment: Measuring cylinder (tall), Tray, Measuring cylinder, Safety screen. Chemicals: Hydrogen peroxide, Potassium iodide, Washing-up liquid. Procedure: Stand a tall measuring cylinder in a tray. Add 50 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide and a squirt of washing-up liquid. Quickly pour in 10 cm³ of potassium iodide solution. Stand back and observe. Observations: Instant eruption of foam; Foam is warm and may be tinged yellow; A glowing splint relights in the foam Explanation: Iodide ions catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. The oxygen gas is trapped by the detergent as foam. The catalyst is not used up. Equation: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (catalysed by I⁻) Conclusion: Catalysts speed up reactions without being consumed; the reaction is strongly exothermic. Safety: Peroxide bleaches skin — wear gloves and goggles.

name: Golden Rain Precipitation
description: Two colourless solutions combine into glittering gold crystals.
info: Two colourless solutions combine into glittering gold crystals. Equipment: Beakers, Bunsen burner, Tripod stand, Wire gauze, Stirring rod. Chemicals: Lead(II) nitrate, Potassium iodide, Distilled water. Procedure: Mix equal volumes of lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions. Observe the instant yellow precipitate. Heat gently until the precipitate dissolves. Allow to cool slowly in a dark place and observe. Observations: Instant bright yellow precipitate; Precipitate dissolves on heating; Shimmering gold hexagonal plates fall like rain on cooling Explanation: Lead ions and iodide ions form insoluble lead iodide. Its solubility increases with temperature, so slow cooling grows large, flat crystals that glint as they tumble. Equation: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ + 2KNO₃ Conclusion: Precipitation reactions follow solubility rules; crystal size depends on how slowly the solution cools. Safety: Lead compounds are toxic. Gloves on; dispose of as hazardous waste.

name: Testing for Halide Ions
description: Identify chloride, bromide and iodide by precipitate colour.
info: Identify chloride, bromide and iodide by precipitate colour. Equipment: Test tubes, Dropping pipettes, Test tube rack. Chemicals: Silver nitrate, Sodium chloride, Potassium iodide, Dilute nitric acid. Procedure: Add a few drops of dilute nitric acid to the unknown solution. Add silver nitrate solution drop by drop. Note the colour of any precipitate. Observations: Chloride → white precipitate; Bromide → cream precipitate; Iodide → yellow precipitate Explanation: Silver halides are insoluble in water. The precipitate colour deepens down the group as the halide ion becomes larger and more polarisable. Equation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl ; Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI Conclusion: Silver nitrate is a reliable test for halide ions; nitric acid removes interfering carbonate ions. Safety: Silver nitrate stains skin black for days — gloves recommended.

name: Metals in Acid
description: Compare how fast different metals fizz in dilute acid.
info: Compare how fast different metals fizz in dilute acid. Equipment: Test tubes, Test tube rack, Stopwatch, Wooden splint. Chemicals: Hydrochloric acid, Magnesium, Zinc, Iron. Procedure: Add 5 cm³ of dilute acid to three test tubes. Add a small piece of each metal to its own tube. Rank the metals by rate of bubbling. Collect gas from the fastest tube and test with a lit splint. Observations: Magnesium: very fast bubbles, warm; Zinc: steady bubbles; Iron: slow bubbles; Squeaky pop with a lit splint Explanation: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from acids. The more reactive the metal, the faster electrons are transferred and the faster the gas forms. Equation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ Conclusion: Order of reactivity: Mg > Zn > Fe. Hydrogen gas gives a squeaky pop. Safety: Keep flames away from the test tubes while gas is forming.

name: pH Rainbow
description: Build a full colour scale using universal indicator and household substances.
info: Build a full colour scale using universal indicator and household substances. Equipment: Test tubes, Test tube rack, Dropping pipettes. Chemicals: Universal indicator, Hydrochloric acid, Ethanoic acid, Distilled water, Sodium bicarbonate, Sodium hydroxide. Procedure: Half fill five test tubes with each solution. Add three drops of universal indicator to each. Arrange in order of colour and estimate pH. Observations: HCl → red (pH 1); Vinegar → orange (pH 3); Water → green (pH 7); Baking soda → blue-green (pH 8–9); NaOH → purple (pH 14) Explanation: Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that each change colour at a different pH, so the combined colour shifts gradually across the scale. Equation: HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ Conclusion: Strong acids and alkalis sit at the ends of the scale; weak ones sit closer to neutral. Safety: Handle NaOH and HCl with goggles on.

name: The pH Scale
description: Measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, from 0 to 14.
info: pH is a measure of hydrogen ion concentration. Each step down the scale means ten times more H⁺ ions. 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline. Example: Lemon juice ≈ pH 2, pure water = pH 7, oven cleaner ≈ pH 13.

name: Reactivity Series
description: Metals ranked by how readily they lose electrons.
info: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > (C) > Zn > Fe > (H) > Cu > Ag > Au. A metal higher in the series can displace one below it from a compound. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids. Example: Zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate, but copper cannot displace zinc.

name: Exothermic & Endothermic
description: Reactions that release or absorb heat energy.
info: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings (temperature rises) — combustion, neutralisation, displacement. Endothermic reactions take in energy (temperature falls) — thermal decomposition, citric acid + baking soda. Example: A hand warmer is exothermic; an instant cold pack is endothermic.

name: Precipitation
description: Two solutions react to form an insoluble solid.
info: When ions that form an insoluble compound meet in solution, the solid "falls out" as a precipitate. Solubility rules predict which combinations will do this — all nitrates are soluble, most carbonates and hydroxides are not. Example: Silver nitrate + sodium chloride → white silver chloride precipitate.

name: Catalysts
description: Substances that speed up reactions without being used up.
info: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. Because it is regenerated, only a tiny amount is needed and it can be recovered at the end. Example: Manganese dioxide or iodide ions speed up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

name: Gas Tests
description: Simple tests to identify common gases.
info: Hydrogen — lit splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen — relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky. Chlorine — bleaches damp litmus paper. Ammonia — turns damp red litmus blue. Example: Zinc in acid gives a gas that pops: it must be hydrogen.

name: Neutralisation
description: Acid + base → salt + water.
info: H⁺ ions from the acid react with OH⁻ ions from the base to form water. The remaining ions form a salt whose name comes from the metal in the base and the acid used (hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate). Example: Antacid tablets neutralise excess stomach acid.

name: Indicators
description: Dyes that change colour with pH.
info: Litmus: red in acid, blue in alkali. Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in alkali. Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali. Universal indicator: full rainbow. Example: Phenolphthalein is used in titrations because its end-point is very sharp.

name: Acetic Anhydride
description: A clear, pungent liquid acid anhydride widely utilized in organic chemistry as an acetylating agent for synthesizing esters like aspirin.
info: Reacts with alcohols and phenols faster and more completely than carboxylic acids without forming water as a byproduct, making it the preferred reagent for producing acetylsalicylic acid from salicylic acid.

name: Salicylic Acid
description: A crystalline beta hydroxy acid (BHA) containing both a carboxylic acid group and an ortho-phenolic hydroxyl group. Crucial precursor for pharmaceuticals and skincare.
info: Synthesized industrially via the Kolbe-Schmitt reaction from sodium phenolate and carbon dioxide under pressure. Esterification of its phenolic -OH produces aspirin, while esterification of its -COOH produces methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen).

name: Copper(II) Carbonate
description: A vibrant turquoise-green basic carbonate compound resembling natural malachite mineral. Decomposes upon heating into black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide.
info: Commonly used in thermal decomposition demonstrations: green CuCO₃ turns completely black (CuO) when heated in a test tube while evolved CO₂ turns limewater milky.

name: Calcium Carbide
description: A greyish-black crystalline solid produced industrially in electric arc furnaces. Reacts vigorously with water to generate acetylene (ethyne) gas.
info: The hydrolysis reaction CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂ produces flammable acetylene gas used for oxy-acetylene welding torches and carbide miner lamps.

name: Sodium Borohydride
description: A versatile white solid reducing agent used in organic and medicinal chemistry to selectively reduce aldehydes and ketones to primary and secondary alcohols.
info: Milder and safer to handle than lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH₄), NaBH₄ can be used in protic solvents like methanol and water without violent decomposition.

name: Soxhlet Extractor
description: A specialized laboratory glassware assembly designed for continuous, automated solid-liquid extraction of sparingly soluble compounds from solid matrices.
info: The sample is placed inside a permeable porous thimble. Distilled solvent vapors bypass the thimble, condense in a reflux condenser, and drip onto the solid. When solvent reaches the siphon arm level, it automatically siphons back into the boiling flask, repeating the cycle continuously.

name: Dean-Stark Trap
description: A glass apparatus used in synthetic organic chemistry to continuously collect and remove water formed during condensation reactions like esterification.
info: Solvent and co-distilled water vaporize as an azeotrope into the condenser. The condensate separates into two layers in the trap: the denser water sinks to the bottom where it can be measured and drained, while the organic solvent overflows back into the reaction flask.

name: Reflux Condenser
description: A double-walled glass tube with an internal cooling coil or jacket that condenses hot vapors back into a liquid, returning them to the boiling flask.
info: Refluxing allows organic reaction mixtures to be heated at their boiling temperature indefinitely without losing volatile reactants or solvents to the atmosphere.

name: Buchner Funnel & Filter Flask
description: A heavy porcelain or polypropylene funnel with a perforated plate, mounted with a rubber cone onto a thick-walled sidearm vacuum filter flask.
info: Connected to a water aspirator or vacuum pump to draw liquids through filter paper under reduced pressure, drying crystalline precipitates dozens of times faster than gravity filtration.

name: Rotary Evaporator (Rotovap)
description: An automated instrument that gently removes volatile solvents from non-volatile reaction products under reduced pressure and controlled rotation in a heated water bath.
info: Lowering the system pressure depresses the boiling point of the solvent, while motorized flask rotation creates a thin fluid film for rapid evaporation without boiling bumping.

name: Gas Syringe
description: A precision ground-glass syringe with milliliter volume calibrations used to accurately collect and measure volumes of gas evolved during chemical reactions.
info: The ground-glass plunger moves smoothly with minimal friction as gas enters, allowing real-time rate measurements (e.g. rate of CO₂ evolution from calcium carbonate and acid).

name: Melting Point Apparatus
description: An analytical testing device used to determine the exact melting temperature and purity range of solid crystalline substances.
info: Pure organic compounds exhibit sharp melting points spanning less than 1°C. Impurities depress the melting point and broaden the melting interval.

name: Laboratory Desiccator
description: A heavy, sealable glass or plastic enclosure containing a desiccant bed in the lower compartment to preserve samples in a dry atmosphere.
info: Used to cool hot ignited crucibles and store hygroscopic analytical standards in a moisture-free environment before weighing on analytical balances.

name: Magnetic Stirrer with Hotplate
description: An electronically controlled benchtop heating unit equipped with a rotating internal magnet that drives an immersed PTFE-coated stir bar.
info: Provides uniform heating and constant vortex agitation without requiring external shafts, ensuring steady dissolution and preventing localized hotspots in reaction vessels.
